Conflicts cannot be avoided, so data loss is inevitable

questions.explanation: A replicated store cannot leave siblings unresolved forever, but automatic last-write-wins may lose valid updates. When the database cannot merge domain values correctly, the application must preserve causality and define a safe merge.

questions.question: How does last-write-wins resolve concurrent values?

options.text: Keep the value with the greatest timestamp and discard the rest
Merge all concurrent values; mandatory in Riak, optional in Cassandra
Pick the lowest timestamp; optional in both
Store all versions as siblings; mandatory in Cassandra

questions.explanation: Concurrent clients provide no causal order, so a timestamp invents an arbitrary winner. Cassandra always uses this policy and Riak can opt into it. It guarantees convergence but may silently discard acknowledged writes, especially under clock skew.

questions.question: State the cost of LWW, including the claim most readers miss.

options.text: It converges, but silently discards concurrent writes that were acknowledged
It only ever discards writes that were genuinely concurrent with one another
It never discards a write at all; it merely reorders them by their timestamps
It costs nothing, because convergence comes free with timestamp comparison

questions.explanation: So LWW is not merely lossy for concurrent writes — clock skew can make it lose non-concurrent ones too.

questions.question: What is the only safe way to use a database with LWW?

options.text: Write each key only once and treat it as immutable, as with a UUID key
Synchronize every clock with NTP and rely on wall-clock timestamps instead
Apply last-write-wins to reads only, and resolve write conflicts in the app
Set w equal to n, so that every replica agrees before a write is accepted

questions.explanation: LWW can discard concurrent writes to the same key. Giving every write a fresh immutable key, such as a UUID, prevents two writes from competing for that key and removes the destructive conflict.

questions.question: What makes one operation happen before another in a distributed system, and when are two operations concurrent?

options.text: B happens after A if B knows about, depends on, or builds upon A; otherwise they are concurrent
A happens before B if A's timestamp is smaller; concurrency means equal timestamps
A happens before B if A was sent from a lower-numbered node; concurrency means same node
A happens before B whenever A committed first, so true concurrency cannot arise

questions.explanation: Causality is based on information flow, not wall-clock timestamps. If B observed or depended on A, then A happened before B; if neither operation could know about the other, they are concurrent.

questions.question: Of two operations where one increments a value the other inserted, and two where neither client knows of the other, which pair is concurrent?

options.text: The increment pair is causal; the mutually unaware pair is the concurrent one
The increment pair is the concurrent one; the mutually unaware pair is causal
Both pairs are concurrent, since neither operation builds on the other one
Both pairs are causally dependent, so concurrency arises in neither of them

questions.explanation: An increment derived from an inserted value depends on that insert, so the operations are causally ordered. When neither client has observed the other's write, neither operation happens before the other and they are concurrent.

questions.question: Must two operations overlap in time for a replicated system to treat them as concurrent?

options.text: Concurrency means mutual unawareness, not overlap in time
Concurrency is defined purely by overlap on a wall clock
Relativity leaves concurrency undefinable in software systems
The speed of light sets the minimum window for concurrency

questions.explanation: Computer systems are more permissive about concurrency than physics, because the network can fail to deliver knowledge even when light had time to.

questions.question: A cart initially contains [milk]. Another client concurrently adds [eggs], while client 1 writes [milk, flour] based on version 1. What does the server retain?

options.text: Version 1 supersedes [milk] but is concurrent with [eggs], so both are kept
It overwrites both [milk] and [eggs], leaving [milk, flour] as the only value
It rejects the write outright, because version 1 is already stale by then
It keeps all three of the values as siblings for the client to merge later

questions.explanation: The version number tells the server which prior state the client observed. The new value supersedes that ancestor, while the unseen [eggs] branch remains a concurrent sibling that must be merged rather than overwritten.

questions.question: What does a graph of the shopping-cart versions and their causal dependencies reveal about stale clients and lost writes?

options.text: It shows causal order and that stale clients need not lose writes
It shows the physical network topology, proving all writes were serialized
It shows wall-clock timestamps, proving the writes were not concurrent
It shows that some writes are lost, which is unavoidable

questions.explanation: The dependency graph identifies which versions descend from others and which are concurrent. A stale client may create another branch, but preserving all concurrent branches avoids silently losing its write.

questions.question: State the rules of the version-number algorithm. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The server maintains a version number for every key, increments it every time that key is written, and stores the new version number along with the value written
When a client reads a key, the server returns all values that have not been overwritten, as well as the latest version number. A client must read a key before writing

When a client writes a key it must include the version number from the prior read, and it must merge together all values that it received in the prior read (the response from a write request can be like a read, returning all current values, which allows chaining several writes)
On receiving a write, the server discards every earlier version of that key and retains only the newest value it has so far seen

questions.explanation: Discarding everything would destroy siblings. The genuine rule is that a write with a particular version number overwrites all values at that version or below, but must keep any higher-numbered values as siblings. Crucially, the server can determine whether two operations are concurrent by looking at the version numbers — it does not need to interpret the value itself, so the value could be any data structure. A write without a version number is concurrent with all other writes, so it will not overwrite anything and will just be returned as one of the values on subsequent reads.

questions.question: Riak calls concurrent values siblings. Merging [milk, flour, eggs, bacon] with [eggs, milk, ham], what is the result and what detail is worth noting?

options.text: The union gives [milk, flour, eggs, bacon, ham] with no duplicates
The merge yields [eggs, milk, ham] because it has the higher version
The merge duplicates milk and eggs, giving seven items
The siblings cannot be merged without losing data

questions.explanation: This is essentially the same problem as conflict resolution in multi-leader replication: you could pick one value based on a version number or timestamp (last write wins), but that implies losing data, so you may need to do something more intelligent in application code. The algorithm ensures that no data is silently dropped, at the cost of requiring clients to clean up afterward by merging the concurrently written values.

questions.question: Where does union merging break, and what is the fix called?

options.text: Removals reappear, so deletions need a tombstone marker instead
It breaks on additions; the fix is a version vector
It breaks on updates; the fix is last write wins
It does not break; union merging is always correct

questions.explanation: Merging siblings in application code is complex and error-prone, so Riak's CRDT datatype support can automatically merge siblings in sensible ways, including preserving deletions.

questions.question: Why is a single version number insufficient with multiple replicas, and what replaces it?

options.text: One version number per replica per key, collected into a version vector
A single version number is sufficient; version vectors are an optimization
Timestamps replace version numbers when there are multiple replicas
A global counter replaces the per-key version number

questions.explanation: Per-replica counters are what let a node distinguish 'I've seen this' from 'this is news to me'.

questions.question: Name the interesting version vector variant, the system using it, and Riak's name for the encoded form.

options.text: The dotted version vector, used in Riak 2.0 as a causal context string
The vector clock, used in Cassandra; Riak calls the encoding a digest
The Lamport timestamp, used in Voldemort; Riak calls it a hint
The hybrid logical clock, used in Riak 1.0; Riak calls it a tombstone

questions.explanation: Causal context travelling with the client is what makes cross-replica read-then-write safe.

questions.question: What cross-replica operation do version vectors make safe, and what is the caveat?

options.text: Read from one replica and write to another, while still merging siblings
They make it safe to write to any replica with no siblings ever created
They make reads strongly consistent, with no caveat
They eliminate the need for application-level merging

questions.explanation: The receiving replica can tell which versions the client observed and which writes are concurrent, so switching replicas does not silently overwrite unseen data. Safety does not eliminate application-level merging.

questions.question: The final box makes a terminology correction. What is it?

options.text: Also called a vector clock, though the two are not quite the same
Vector clocks and version vectors are identical terms
Vector clocks are the right structure for comparing replica state
Implementations use neither term, preferring to speak of causal context instead

questions.explanation: The names are often conflated, but version vectors track a version per replica for a data item, while vector clocks are the broader causal-ordering concept. For Dynamo-style conflict detection, 'version vector' is more precise.

questions.question: Which purposes can replication serve? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: High availability — keeping the system running when machines or a datacenter fail
Disconnected operation — allowing work to continue through a network interruption
Lower geographic latency and greater read scalability by serving users and read traffic from replicas
Guaranteed preservation of every acknowledged write even when replication is asynchronous

questions.explanation: Replication supports availability, offline work, geographic latency reduction, and read scalability. Asynchronous followers cannot guarantee that every acknowledged write survives leader loss, but they can absorb read traffic when the application tolerates or controls staleness.
